definition: Elusive means hard to find, catch, or pin down.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word elusive. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know elusive should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: A perfect pizza crust stayed elusive all winter, no matter how Ben timed the rise or juggled the oven racks.
A shy cat merely hangs back and can be coaxed out; elusive goes further - the thing actively slips every attempt to catch it.
Untraceable is the extreme: an elusive signal keeps slipping your instruments, but an untraceable one leaves nothing behind to follow at all.

Slippery is the plain-talk version: the thing wriggles out of your grip just as you close it - an eel, an excuse, a definition. Elusive covers the same escape in more formal dress and stretches further, to anything that stays beyond reach: a cure, a culprit, a full night's sleep.

Shadowy means glimpsed only at the edges and never seen plainly - a shadowy figure, a shadowy backer. Elusive is about escape, not dimness: an elusive thing can be vivid and unmistakable yet never where you reach. Shadowy blurs the view; elusive defeats the grab.

The whine started the moment the lights went off.
For an hour Jo stalked the bedroom with a rolled magazine - lamp on, silence; lamp off, the whine at her ear.
The mosquito was maddeningly elusive: unmistakably there, and never once where she looked.
Elusive is exact because the mosquito really exists and actively escapes capture - that combination is the word's core.
It is not imaginary and not merely uncommon; it is present, close, and forever slipping the grasp.
Anything that behaves that way - a name, a melody, an agreement - earns the word.
Elusive is for things with real existence that keep escaping - an animal, a word, an agreement, sleep.
Nebulous, its neighbor in this unit, means the thing never had an outline to begin with.
If you could catch it if only it held still, it is elusive; if there is nothing solid to catch, it is nebulous.

In 1911, a crate of silent-film reels vanished somewhere between a Chicago studio and a Denver theater.
For film historians, the crate became the most elusive prize in early cinema: every decade brought a promising lead, and every lead went cold.
Archivists traced shipping manifests, auction lots, and a retired projectionist's letters, yet the reels stayed out of reach.
The frustrating part, one researcher wrote, was that the crate was no ghost story -- the paperwork proved it existed, right up to the last rail depot.
A century on, the search continues, its object as real and as unreachable as ever.
